title: A private-school website that helps families take the next step
description: A practical guide to private-school website design for admissions and marketing. Covers page architecture, age and programme fit, curriculum pages, admissions steps, visiting, fees, privacy, and how to keep current-parent resources separate from prospective-family content.
summary: A good private-school website gives prospective families a clear admissions path: who the school is for, the curriculum, how to visit and apply, and honest guidance on fees. Current-parent resources belong in a separate area. Design should be beautiful, fast and accessible, not an awards exercise.
takeaways: Design the site around a prospective family's next step, not around the school's internal structure: age and programme fit, curriculum, admissions steps, visiting and fees.
Keep current-parent resources separate from admissions marketing, so the public pages stay focused on the families you are trying to recruit.
Choose craft and accessibility over decoration: a beautiful, fast, readable site builds more trust than a complicated one.

sections.title: What the website is for
sections.body:
A private-school website has one job above all others: help a family who does not yet know the school decide whether to take the next step. That step might be an enquiry, an open-house visit or an application. Everything on the public site should either move a family towards one of those actions or answer the honest questions they will have on the way.

That sounds obvious, but many school sites are organised around the school's internal life rather than the family's decision. The result is a homepage full of news for people who already attend, programme pages written for colleagues, and admissions information buried under three levels of navigation. If you start the project by asking what a visiting parent needs to understand, in what order, the design decisions get much easier. The private-school website is a recruitment tool first and a noticeboard second.

sections.title: Prospective families and current families are different readers
sections.body:
A private school serves at least two distinct audiences online, and they want almost opposite things. Prospective parents want a clear story, a sense of fit, and a confident path to apply. Current parents want the calendar, the lunch menu, the uniform guide, report access and the newsletter. Mixing those two streams on the same public pages usually means neither audience is well served.

The practical answer is separation. The main navigation and homepage speak to families who are choosing. The current-family material lives behind a clear "Current families" or "Parents" area, and ideally behind a sign-in where the content is genuinely private. That split also helps design: the public pages can be simpler, more visual and more persuasive, because they no longer have to double as the school's filing cabinet.

sections.title: A sensible page architecture
sections.body:
Before any visual design, the site needs an information architecture that matches the family's questions. For most independent schools, a sensible public structure looks like this:

  • Home: a short, confident statement of who the school is for, supported by photography that shows the actual school experience.
  • About: mission, values, history and leadership, written for an outsider.
  • Admissions: the steps, key dates, who to contact, and the enquiry form.
  • Visit: open-house dates, tour booking, directions and what to expect.
  • Academics or Programmes: by division or age, for example early years, elementary and high school, each with curriculum and approach.
  • Student life: athletics, arts, clubs and the culture between classes.
  • Fees and financial aid: whatever the school is prepared to publish, clearly framed.
  • Current families: a separate area or portal entry point.

This is not the only right answer, but it is a good test: if a proposed page does not fit naturally anywhere here, ask who it is for. My broader approach to website design starts the same way, with the reader's job to do.

sections.title: Make the admissions steps obvious
sections.body:
An unclear admissions path can leave an interested family unsure what to do next. The family is interested, but the path from interest to application is vague, which makes it harder for them to continue. A strong admissions page does three things: it shows the process as a small number of plain steps, it makes the first step very easy, and it tells the family what happens after each step.

The first step should ask for very little. A sample enquiry form might look like this:

  • Intended entry grade and year; leave the child’s name and records for the school’s approved application process.
  • Parent or guardian name and email.
  • Optional phone number and one open question, such as what the family is looking for.

Keep the first-contact form short. Additional information can be requested later through the school’s approved admissions system. The page should also make visiting feel natural, because for most families the visit, not the website, is where the real decision happens. A clear "Book a tour" or "Join an open house" action belongs on the admissions page and in the navigation.

sections.title: Show curriculum and age fit for real
sections.body:
Parents are not only buying a school. They are buying a particular education for a particular child at a particular age. A generic "excellent academics" claim does not help them. What helps is a page for each stage or programme that answers: who is this for, what will my child study, how is it taught, and what comes next.

For an elementary page, that might mean the reading and numeracy approach, the role of specialists, and how much time is spent outside. For a high-school page, it might mean course breadth, graduation requirements, post-secondary preparation and support for students who need it. If the school offers something distinctive, such as a faith foundation, an outdoor programme or an arts stream, that belongs on the programme page, not only on the homepage. The fit has to feel real enough that a family can say either yes, this is us, or no, it is not.

sections.title: Handle fees honestly
sections.body:
Fees are the topic every school handles carefully, and the website has to follow the school's decision rather than make one for it. Some schools publish full tuition tables. Some publish a range or a starting point. Some prefer to discuss cost only in conversation. I would publish the tuition and compulsory charges where possible, with the applicable school year, payment arrangements and a clear route to ask about assistance. What does not work is pretending the question does not exist, because it is one of the first things a family wants to know.

Whatever the school can say, say it plainly and put it where people will look. If there is bursary or financial-aid support, name it and explain how to ask. If the school would rather talk first, the page can say so honestly and offer the next step. Make the next step concrete: identify the admissions contact, what information is available before a visit, and how the family can request a full fee breakdown.

sections.title: Safeguarding, privacy and trust
sections.body:
School websites collect personal information about children and families, so the forms and systems behind them deserve real care. In British Columbia, guidance from the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner asks private organisations to collect only the personal information they genuinely need, to be clear about the purpose, and to make their privacy practices available. That is sensible advice anywhere, not just in BC.

In practice: do not ask for a student's history, medical details or financial documents on a public enquiry form. Collect the minimum needed to respond, and route anything sensitive through the school's approved systems. Publish or offer a plain-language privacy note so a parent can see what will happen with their information. Trust is built by these small, careful choices as much as by the photography.

sections.title: Craft, beauty and accessibility
sections.body:
A private-school website should be beautiful. Families are choosing an environment for their children, and the quality of the design quietly signals the quality of the care. Good typography, real photography of the school rather than generic stock, confident spacing and an unhurried pace all do persuasive work that no tagline can.

Beauty has to survive contact with real devices, though. The site needs to be fast on a phone, readable in bright light, and usable by everyone. The W3C's easy accessibility checks are a good first review: clear page titles, sensible headings, text alternatives for meaningful images, and enough contrast to read comfortably. An accessible site is usually also a more beautiful one, because both come from the same habit of caring about the reader.

sections.title: Decide these things before you brief a designer
sections.table:
Worksheet: decisions that shape a private-school website
DecisionQuestions to answerWhat it changes on the site
Audience splitWhich content is for prospective families, and which is for current ones?Main navigation, homepage focus, whether a parent area or portal is needed.
Admissions pathWhat are the actual steps, and what should the first contact ask for?Admissions page layout, enquiry form length, tour and open-house calls to action.
Age and programme fitWhich divisions or programmes need their own page?Structure of the academics section and how specific each page can be.
Fees stanceWhat, if anything, can the school publish about tuition and aid?Whether there is a fees page, and how the money question is framed.
Privacy postureWhat personal information is truly needed at each step?Form fields, where sensitive data is collected, and the privacy note.
Design ambitionHow much custom design, photography and video is realistic?Budget, timeline, and whether to start with a focused redesign. My notes on website cost can help frame that conversation.
sections.body:
The best school website projects start before the first design meeting. When the school has already decided who the site is for, what the admissions steps are and how it wants to talk about money, the design work can focus on craft instead of guesswork. Use this worksheet to turn the discussion into decisions before asking for quotes.

Admissions website decisions to settle before design
DecisionWhat to prepareWho checks it
Family fitEntry ages, programmes and the questions families ask before visitingAdmissions lead
Visit and applicationActual steps, dates, response owner and the approved application systemAdmissions team
FeesCurrent-year tuition, compulsory charges, payment options and assistance informationFinance and admissions
Proof and mediaCurrent school photographs and permission records for their intended useSchool communications lead
Current familiesPublic notices, private portal links and an owner for keeping each currentSchool administrator

Assign a person to each decision so missing information does not become a design problem.

Once those decisions are on the table, the design work itself becomes the interesting part: photography, typography, page rhythm and the small details that make a school feel like itself. If you would like to talk through where your current site stands and what the next piece of work should achieve, book a free consultation.

faqs: Should a private school publish its exact tuition fees on the website?

Only if the school is comfortable doing so. Some publish full tables, some give a range or starting point, and some prefer a conversation first. What matters is acknowledging the question plainly, naming any bursary or aid options, and giving the family an honest next step rather than leaving the cost invisible.
How separate should the current-parent area be from the public site?

As separate as the content requires. Public pages should speak to families who are choosing a school. Newsletters, calendars, lunch menus and similar material for enrolled families work best in a clearly labelled parent area, and behind a sign-in when the information is private. This keeps the public admissions pages focused and easier to design well.
What should we prepare before asking a designer for a quote?

Decide the audience split between prospective and current families, outline the real admissions steps, list which programmes need their own page, agree how the school will talk about fees, and gather any existing photography or video. With those decisions made, the conversation with a designer can be about craft and fit rather than guesswork.
